vignette:
He is 21 and already speaks about his life in terms of before and after. Before the war zone, he imagined his work as relief would be difficult but meaningful, something that would test his endurance and confirm his faith in service. He had recently married, and he and his wife had talked often about sacrifice, purpose, and building a life that felt larger than themselves. When he accepted the assignment as a social ministry worker, he carried that conviction with him: that he could go where others could not and bring comfort, food, prayer, and practical help.

The first weeks in the region feel, in his telling, almost unreal in their intensity. He moves through damaged streets, makes lists of needs, distributes supplies, checks on families, and tries to keep his voice steady when children cling to him or adults ask questions he cannot answer. He describes a constant pressure in his body, a readiness for the next explosion, the next siren, the next call for help. Even in those early days, he notices that he sleeps lightly and wakes at the smallest sound. He begins to measure each day not by the hour but by what he has managed to prevent.

The event that changes everything happens during an ordinary task. He is accompanying a small group to deliver aid when the area comes under fire. He remembers the abruptness of it, the impossibility of preparing for it, and the way the world seems to narrow to noise, dust, and the instinct to survive. In the chaos, someone near him is killed. Another person he knows from daily work is badly injured. He recalls seeing blood on the ground, hearing crying that he cannot locate, and feeling his own body move without deliberation as he tries to pull others to cover. He speaks about the moment later with a kind of disbelief, as if it belongs to someone else, though his face tightens when he describes it. What stays with him most is not only fear but helplessness: the sense that he was there to help and could not stop what was happening.

Afterward, he returns to work quickly, partly because there is no time to stop and partly because stopping feels like surrender. He tells himself that the people there still need him. But his mind keeps replaying the attack in fragments. At night he sees flashes of the scene when he closes his eyes, and in the day certain sounds—sharp bangs, distant helicopters, the crack of static on a radio—pull him back into the moment so suddenly that he has to look around to remind himself where he is. He becomes vigilant in a way that is almost exhausting to watch him describe. He checks exits automatically, sits with his back to walls, scans rooftops, and notices every shift in a room. He says he no longer feels relaxed anywhere.

He also grows distant from the parts of life that once felt steady. He loves his wife deeply, but when they talk by phone or video, he finds it hard to explain what he is carrying. He does not want to frighten her, and he does not know how to put the images into language she can bear. Sometimes he is brief and clipped. Sometimes he says too little and then feels guilty for sounding absent. He misses home, yet he also feels strangely detached from it, as if he is watching another life continue without him. He returns to old prayers and familiar verses, but even spiritual practices feel changed by what he has witnessed. He says he believes, but the belief now sits beside anger, grief, and confusion.

In the months that follow, he becomes increasingly jumpy and tired. He startles when doors slam. He avoids news footage, war films, and crowded places that make him feel cornered. He has trouble sleeping because when the room is quiet, the memories become louder. Some nights he wakes already tense, certain for a moment that something terrible is happening again. He tries to push through, maintaining the routines of a social ministry worker—calls, visits, organizing support, listening to other people’s needs—but he notices he is less patient than before and more easily overwhelmed by small demands. He grieves the person who died in front of him, though he rarely says that directly. Instead, he carries a private, persistent sadness, along with a sense that part of him remained there in the dust and smoke.

When he talks now, there is still pride in his work and loyalty to the people he served, but it is mixed with fear that he will never feel entirely safe again. He wants to be useful, to return to the version of himself that could move through the world with certainty, yet he feels changed in ways he cannot fully reverse.
